caveats: A few events prove the machinery, not the forecasting power: every rate here rests on a handful of places for one or two events. One graded place moves a hit rate by tens of points. Read these as a worked, auditable comparison, not a skill estimate. The simulator's traffic is modelled from lane structure, not the historical fleet.

capacity_loss_basis.source: Marine Exchange of Southern California (MESocal) 10 Nov 2021 report, via Western Overseas: https://www.westernoverseas.com/port-congestion-update-11-12-21/ (same report already cited for the 2021-11-10 observed steps in this dataset)
capacity_loss_basis.text: MODELED assumption - not a sourced figure and never to be presented as one. No sourced capacity-loss fraction exists for LA 2021: the source record quantifies queues and waits, not capacity loss, and berth throughput did not collapse (the Port of Los Angeles was on track for a record ~10.7M TEU in 2021, Port of Los Angeles release, 20 Dec 2021), so no throughput-drop derivation is defensible. Model: at the 10 Nov 2021 MESocal snapshot the complex held 109 container ships waiting and 30 at berth; capacity_loss is set to the waiting share of container ships present, 109 / (109 + 30) = 0.78 (rounded to 2 dp) - a stock-share proxy for the share of container-ship flow the berth/landside system was not serving at the peak snapshot, NOT a measured throughput drop. The binding constraint was landside (dwell/driver channel), not berth capacity. Any scorecard printing LA results must print this modeled assumption alongside them. (An earlier version carried capacity_loss as null; the engine then silently substituted its 0.5 default for congestion-kind specs.)
